title: Japan Cancels Hayabusa2 Mission, Ending Planned Close-Up Look at Object Avi Loeb Claims Could Be Soviet Spacecraft
excerpt: Japan’s decision to cancel a planned 2031 encounter with the small object 1998 KY26 has removed the best prospect for obtaining close-up images of its
content:
Japan’s decision to cancel a planned 2031 encounter with the small object 1998 KY26 has removed the best prospect for obtaining close-up images of its surface, according to Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb. He argues that the object could be a defunct Soviet spacecraft, though NASA and other scientists have attributed its unusual motion to natural forces.

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) dropped the Hayabusa2 mission’s planned rendezvous after the spacecraft’s last normally functioning main ion engine malfunctioned in mid-August. In a report to the government’s Space Policy Committee, the agency said the spacecraft no longer had enough thrust to carry out the orbital changes needed to reach KY26. Hayabusa2 is instead being redirected toward a 2028 flyby of asteroid 2015 BM510, according to the Japanese newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun.

Loeb told Fox News Digital that without a spacecraft passing close to KY26, astronomers are unlikely to obtain images detailed enough to distinguish its surface features. Even the James Webb Space Telescope and the largest ground-based telescopes cannot resolve the object into multiple pixels in an image, he said.

The cancellation came shortly after NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on “Fox & Friends” that he had seen no evidence that KY26 was anything other than an asteroid. Loeb disputes that conclusion, saying the object’s acceleration cannot be explained by gravity alone. He has suggested that sunlight reflecting from the panels of the missing Soviet probe Phobos 1 could account for the motion.

Phobos 1 was launched toward Mars in July 1988 but lost contact after a faulty command shut down the spacecraft. Loeb and colleagues have said KY26’s trajectory resembles the probe’s expected path. Loeb has also speculated that a close encounter would reveal identifying markings on the object. That remains an unverified claim; no close-up images have established that KY26 is artificial.

JAXA said the planned route already required an Earth gravity assist. According to the agency’s report, combining usable parts from two damaged engines would still not provide enough thrust for the required maneuvers. Loeb questioned why engineers had not tried a different gravity-assist plan, and said he was surprised the cancellation followed his public comments by only a day or two. He noted, however, that the engine problem had been known for months and acknowledged that the timing could be coincidental.

A NASA orbital study reached a different explanation for the object’s motion. The agency’s Center for Near-Earth Object Studies concluded that forces from sunlight and thermal emissions acting on KY26’s irregular shape could account for its complex trajectory, rather than activity from a comet or a spacecraft.

Loeb said astronomers may still be able to investigate the object remotely with Webb. So far, observations have measured sunlight reflected by KY26. Webb could potentially detect heat emitted by the object, helping researchers estimate its size and surface temperature and study its composition.

He has highlighted two features he considers unusual: KY26 rotates roughly once every five minutes, and it reflects about half the sunlight that reaches it. Loeb said that is much more reflective than a typical rock or iceberg, which he estimated would reflect around 5%. Other scientists have proposed that KY26 is a natural asteroid or comet.

Loeb has argued that if the object were a comet releasing gas, astronomers might expect to see gas or dust around it. He said a visible tail would be expected in the case of dust being pushed away from the Sun by radiation pressure. NASA’s study, by contrast, attributes the measured acceleration to the effects of sunlight and heat on the object’s shape.

KY26’s orbit takes it from a fraction of the Earth–Sun distance to several times that distance, Loeb said, and the object poses no threat of colliding with Earth. He nevertheless urged agencies to remain open to testing unusual explanations when tracking objects in space.

He also pointed to the brief classification of a near-Earth object in January 2025 that was later identified as the Tesla Roadster launched by SpaceX in 2018. The object was recognized after its known flight path was taken into account, Loeb said.

He expressed hope that the Rubin Observatory in Chile will discover many more interstellar objects in the coming decade, giving astronomers opportunities to study whether they are natural bodies or, in rare cases, objects of technological origin.
